title: A small library, thoughtfully built
text: Good documentation feels like a well-kept notebook. There is a clear place to begin, enough space to think, and a useful example just when you need one. The page makes room for the work.

title: A small library, thoughtfully built
text: Imagine a little library of things you want to return to: an essay, a useful function, a question that deserves a second look. Each entry needs a title, a few words of context, and a way to find it again. from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass class Entry: title: str tags: tuple[str, ...] = () library = [Entry("The art of paying attention", ("reading",))] The code uses IBM Plex Mono, with a little more room between lines. Names, punctuation, and indentation stay distinct. Inline expressions such as entry.title belong comfortably in the surrounding text.

title: A small library, thoughtfully built
text: A useful page has a rhythm: a thought, an example, a pause. Headings mark a change of subject. A quieter margin keeps the route through the document visible without competing for attention. A good notebook is a place to think on paper, and a place to find that thought again. The typography specimen shows longer prose and quotations. The code and data page adds tabs, tables, and a folded example.

title: The useful art of returning
text: A passage changes when we return to it. The words are the same, but the questions we bring have become more precise. A note left in the margin is a small invitation to our future self.

title: The useful art of returning
text: Instead of recording everything, keep the question that made you pause. It gives the next reading a place to begin.

title: An example is a little argument
text: A useful example is small enough to hold in mind and complete enough to run. It gives the reader something concrete to question, change, and understand.

title: An example is a little argument
text: def twice(value): return value + value assert twice(21) == 42 The explanation can grow from here, one decision at a time.

title: Make it your own
text: In _smalldocs.yml: theme: nocturne toc: true code-copy: true For a _quarto.yml built by SmallDocs, put theme: nocturne under smalldocs:. The normal SmallDocs navigation control switches between the two color modes.

title: Make it your own
text: quarto add rahuldave/smalldocs-nocturne format: nocturne-html: toc: true

title: Make it your own
text: The repository contains the full theme source in src/, font files and Bootstrap in vendor/, the build scripts, tests, and these example pages. Run sh scripts/build.sh to rebuild the CSS and Quarto Sass. The compiled files in _extensions/nocturne/ are committed too, so installing the theme needs no CSS compiler.

title: Make it your own
text: Midnight ink, warm brass, and a literary serif. Made for focused reading, with a pearl-paper light mode. All code uses IBM Plex Mono, bundled with the theme. The source and examples have an MIT license; the fonts retain their SIL Open Font License notices.

title: Make it your own
text: The current theme does not add a fixed label above your title. To restore that effect, create styles.css in your site folder and add it to _smalldocs.yml: theme: nocturne css: styles.css Put this rule in styles.css, and change the quoted label to suit your site: html .quarto-title::before { content: "THE NOTEBOOK · VOL. 01"; display: block; font: 400 .59rem var(--bs-font-monospace); letter-spacing: .14em; color: var(--e-accent); margin-bottom: 1.5rem; } The rule adds the same decorative text above every title. For text that changes with the page, use its content or subtitle: in its front matter. Remove the CSS rule to turn the label off. The theme handbook describes this theme and shows how to connect your stylesheet with SmallDocs and Quarto.

title: The shape of a good page
text: The first obligation of a page is to be read. A comfortable line, a generous margin, and an unhurried rhythm do much of the work. The details become noticeable through their consistency: the distance above a heading, the weight of a rule, the way a link sits inside a sentence. This paragraph contains emphasis, a stronger point, and a link to the code specimen. A reference to library.find() takes its place in the sentence without changing the rhythm. Numbers such as 0123456789 and punctuation — dashes, “quotation marks,” and parentheses — should feel at home together.

title: The shape of a good page
text: The hierarchy comes from a few deliberate changes in size and weight. A heading should help a reader skim the page and then settle back into the text.

title: The shape of a good page
text: Subheadings stay clear at a smaller scale. They introduce a brief explanation, an exception, or the next step in an example.

title: The shape of a good page
text: Start with something concrete: a question, a small example, or a result. Explain enough for the reader to make sense of it. Leave a useful route to the next idea. A list can be brief. A longer entry wraps naturally, with its continuation aligned to its own text. The indentation keeps the page easy to scan. Nested detail should earn its place. Read a little, think a little, and write something worth returning to. A notebook grows through attention, one useful page at a time.

title: The shape of a good page
text: A footnote is a good home for a detail that would interrupt a sentence. It remains available when the reader wants it. Quiet colors and clear boundaries give an aside its own place on the page. An exception needs enough contrast to be found again when it matters. This note folds away. Its title remains a useful signpost, and the detail is one click away. The next specimen shows code and data in the same typographic system. These demos use ordinary footnotes. Margin notes are supported by the theme too: set reference-location: margin, as in the Tufte demo.
